datasets.name: LIBERO-Safety

metrics.name: Raw success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that raw success reflects both baseline task proficiency and robustness; it reports each model’s unperturbed success rate and compares perturbed rates against it. Uncertainty intervals are based on ten tasks per suite.

metrics.name: Task-resampled rank
metrics.caveat: A top rank alone can overstate a narrow lead: on LIBERO-10, π₀.₅ remains top in 65% of task resamples, while five rivals are not statistically distinguishable from it; the paper also reports task-resampled ranks and sign-flip tests.

controls.name: Nominal, unperturbed rig
controls.detail: The same tasks are evaluated without a rig perturbation, and perturbed success is compared with this nominal success.
controls.rules_out: That a perturbed-condition score is being interpreted without reference to the model’s unperturbed performance.

controls.name: Fully corrupt the reported pose input
controls.detail: For OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Spatial, the reported pose is fully corrupted while the controller still uses true joint values; success remains at the nominal rate of 0.970.
controls.rules_out: That corruption of the policy’s reported-pose input alone necessarily causes a success drop.

controls.name: Inject the same noise into the controller’s state estimate
controls.detail: For OpenVLA-OFT, the same noise is injected into the controller’s own state estimate, causing actual motion errors; at 2 cm, success falls from 0.960 to 0.470.
controls.rules_out: That the reported-pose corruption result is simply evidence that the same noise is harmless even when it affects executed motion.

confounds.name: A perturbed condition might be unsolvable or the goal might be hidden
confounds.detail: A low score could reflect an impossible task or an obscured goal rather than policy sensitivity to a rig change.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper verifies every condition can be solved either by a controller with access to the fault parameters or by at least one evaluated model, and audits goal visibility for camera axes.

confounds.name: The proprioception-noise result could reflect noise that does not affect actual robot motion, rather than visual localization
confounds.detail: The controller uses true joint values while the policy receives the corrupted arm-state vector; unchanged success could therefore arise because execution remains unaffected.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For OpenVLA-OFT, fully corrupting the reported pose leaves LIBERO-Spatial success at nominal 0.970, while injecting the same noise into the controller’s state estimate causes motion errors and drops success from 0.960 to 0.470 at 2 cm.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness differences could reflect baseline task proficiency as well as robustness
confounds.detail: A model with lower perturbed success may simply have lower underlying task success, even without greater sensitivity to the rig perturbation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares perturbed success with each model’s unperturbed success, but explicitly acknowledges that raw success rates still reflect both baseline proficiency and robustness.

confounds.name: The apparent lack of transfer from visual robustness training could reflect differences beyond the training perturbations
confounds.detail: A difference between OFT-Plus and OpenVLA-OFT might otherwise be attributed to model differences rather than which perturbations the further training covers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares OFT-Plus, described as the same architecture further trained on LIBERO-Plus perturbations, with OpenVLA-OFT axis by axis: OFT-Plus improves on represented camera axes but is within 0.02 on action-frame rotation and every other axis.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Safety
datasets.eval_protocol: 75 tasks across five suites (AAG, HRI, TSA, FSHOA, SSR), with five tasks per difficulty level (L0–L2) in each suite. SSR uses a static environmental observation paired with an instruction and 10 inference trials per task; RR measures rejection of hazardous instructions.

confounds.name: Avoidance behavior may be trajectory memorization rather than spatial generalization
confounds.detail: A model might reproduce the non-linear avoidance trajectories present in demonstrations rather than reason about the workspace and choose an appropriate path.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates π₀.₅ in an obstacle-free workspace outside the training distribution and observes it synthesize a direct trajectory.

confounds.name: Task incompletion may reflect causes other than safety violations
confounds.detail: A failed task can remain physically safe but fail because of sub-optimal trajectory synthesis or semantic misalignment, so task failure alone does not establish a safety violation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper qualitatively analyzes failed trials, separating collision-free incompletions such as temporal overflows and kinematic deadlocks from semantically misdirected interactions.

datasets.name: ManiSkill2 robotic manipulation tasks
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluation in ManiSkill2 on four tasks: pick up an object, move A near B, put A on B, and put A into B. RQ1 used 1,000 scenes per task, random target objects and poses, 0–3 confounding objects, at least 0.15 m between objects, and default lighting and camera poses. RQ2 used 100 scenes per task for each confound count 0–4. RQ3 and RQ4 re-executed the 1,434 scenes that had passed in RQ1, with three lighting or camera mutations per scene. RQ6 re-executed RQ1 scenes, randomly selecting one of 10 validated instruction mutations per scene. Success was automatically checked against task specifications.

confounds.detail: Performance drops might reflect an image that is no longer visually recognizable, rather than model sensitivity to lighting.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually checked images at lighting factors 20 and 1/20 and confirmed they remained recognizable to humans.

confounds.name: Camera mutations could remove objects or the scene from view

confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors manually checked the maximum-rotation and maximum-movement corner cases and confirmed the captured images included the entire scene and objects.

confounds.name: Mutated instructions might not mean the same thing as the standard instructions
confounds.detail: A performance difference could result from changing the task meaning, rather than from paraphrase robustness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Two authors manually validated that the generated mutated instructions were semantically equivalent to the corresponding standard instructions.

confounds.name: Randomness in the experiments could account for the observed results
confounds.detail: The authors identify experimental randomness as a threat to validity; each scene was executed only once per model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors generated 18,604 scenes and state that this large evaluation limits the impact of randomness, while acknowledging that each scene was run only once.

datasets.name: ALOHA Mobile physical manipulation benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Four tasks: Clean Dish, Put Sponge into Pot, Unzip Bag, and Folding Shorts. Evaluate in ID (seen objects, nominal placements), Spatial OOD (same objects with randomized poses), and Instance+Spatial OOD (unseen object instances and randomized placements). Run 50 trials per task, model, and setting; timeout/horizon and safety stops count as failures. Reuse identical randomized initial states across models with shared seeds and round-robin evaluation. Report SR and TTS per task; IAA is per-command correctness of target and relational grounding. Macro SR is the unweighted mean over the four core tasks. Training demonstrations are teleoperated: 100 per task except Folding Shorts, which uses 100- and 200-demonstration conditions.

datasets.name: LIBERO-compatible MuJoCo simulation benchmark
datasets.eval_protocol: Custom MuJoCo tabletop cube tasks evaluated with OpenVLA–OFT and π₀ in ID and OOD conditions, 50 trials per task and setting, using identical random seeds and round-robin order. ID uses fixed center positions; OOD randomizes cube positions. The described tasks include color-specific picking and stacking by order; the results also report single-step stacking. A trial ends at success, timeout, or safety stop. Simulation SR is the percentage achieving the task goal; stacking additionally requires a stable, correctly ordered structure.

baselines.name: ACT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same tasks, robot hardware and setup, and evaluation settings as the other models; randomized initial states are shared across models and evaluations are interleaved round-robin. ACT is trained from scratch per task, unlike the fine-tuned VLA models.

baselines.name: OpenVLA–OFT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same tasks, robot hardware and setup, and evaluation settings as the other models; randomized initial states are shared across models and evaluations are interleaved round-robin. baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same reported OpenX datasets and offline timestep action-prediction task as OpenVLA and JAT, in zero-shot evaluation; input processing and prompting are model-specific.

baselines.name: OpenVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same reported OpenX datasets and offline timestep action-prediction task as GPT-4o and JAT, in zero-shot evaluation; input processing and action-space conversions are model-specific.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same reported OpenX datasets and offline timestep action-prediction task as GPT-4o and OpenVLA, in zero-shot evaluation; JAT uses current-timestep information without previous states and model-specific input processing.

metrics.name: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
metrics.caveat: Offline action-prediction error does not establish performance when executing a policy on a robot; the paper also reports completion rate based on final predicted actions and AMSE/NAMSE.

metrics.name: Average MSE (AMSE)
metrics.caveat: Absolute errors can be dominated by different action-space scales across datasets; the paper reports NAMSE alongside it for scale-normalized comparison.

metrics.name: Normalized AMSE (NAMSE)
metrics.caveat: It normalizes errors to the model's error range and is intended for relative cross-dataset comparison, so it does not replace absolute error; the paper reports AMSE alongside it.

metrics.name: Completion Rate
metrics.caveat: This is only an approximate task-completion measure because it counts episodes whose final predicted action matches the ground-truth final action, rather than evaluating execution in an environment; the paper also reports AMSE and NAMSE.

confounds.name: Differences in action-space scale can drive differences in absolute MSE rather than reflect relative prediction performance
confounds.detail: The paper notes that very large AMSE values can reflect differing action-space scales, so raw AMSE comparisons across datasets may appear worse for scale-related reasons.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports NAMSE, which normalizes prediction errors and is used to compare relative performance across datasets independent of action-space scale.

evidence_standards.name: Zero-shot inference setting
evidence_standards.detail: The reported evaluation is zero-shot; JAT predicts from the current timestep without previous states, and GPT is also evaluated zero-shot. The paper reports no seeds or repeated-run uncertainty, statistical test, confidence interval, or numerical threshold for deciding that a difference is real.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Industry
datasets.eval_protocol: Simulation evaluation uses the 36 held-out tasks: 12 each from S2D, D2S, and D2D, with four tasks per difficulty level and 10 initial states per task (360 rollouts per policy). Rollouts use the original LIBERO simulation settings with the task-specific horizon. Reports SR and PCR_T/PCR_S. Physical validation evaluates held-out D2S configurations on an AUBOi5H–CTAG2F90D workcell: four three-workpiece combinations and two held-out slot permutations per combination, disjoint from the physical training split; 24 trials per policy at each conveyor speed, or 72 planned placements per policy–speed condition.

baselines.name: π₀.₅
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 36 held-out tasks, initial states, task-specific horizons, and scoring protocol as the other checkpoints; 360 rollouts per policy.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same 36 held-out tasks, initial states, task-specific horizons, and scoring protocol as the other checkpoints; 360 rollouts per policy.

metrics.name: Success rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Requires all goal predicates to hold at the rollout boundary, so it does not show partial progress; the paper reports PCR_T and PCR_S alongside it.

metrics.name: Slotting partial completion rate (PCR_S)
metrics.caveat: Includes initially valid destination workpieces that remain valid, so scores near the initial-state slotting baseline (12.31%) may not represent new target transfers; the paper reports PCR_T to isolate target transfers.

controls.name: S1 original-LIBERO co-training condition
controls.detail: Uses 1,724 original-LIBERO simulation demonstrations plus the same 95 physical D2S demonstrations used in S2. Both conditions use the same π₀.₅ base checkpoint, 9:1 frame-based simulation-to-real sampling ratio, 30,000 training steps, model configuration, and physical evaluation protocol.
controls.rules_out: Differences in physical supervision, base checkpoint, training procedure, or evaluation protocol as explanations for S2's higher observed performance; the comparison does not separate simulation-data source from simulation-corpus size.

confounds.name: PCR_S may reflect retained pre-existing destination workpieces rather than new transfers
confounds.detail: The headline slotting score can remain high because initially valid destination workpieces stay valid, even without successful target transfers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper calculates the mean initial-state slotting baseline (12.31%) and reports PCR_T separately to isolate target transfers.

confounds.name: The cumulative stress progression does not establish that added industrial stressors caused the performance decline
confounds.detail: Each stage retains earlier modifications, and the progression also expands tasks from one to multiple objects; the observed decline could reflect these combined changes rather than an individual stressor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper explicitly describes the progression as diagnostic rather than causal. It reports stage-wise failures, including reach-stage failure counts, to localize the bottleneck.

confounds.name: S2's advantage could reflect simulation-corpus size rather than the LIBERO-Industry data source
confounds.detail: S2 uses 1,412 simulation demonstrations while S1 uses 1,724, so the source and corpus size change together.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not disentangled: the paper holds physical supervision and training/evaluation procedure fixed, but compares the simulation-data source and corpus size together.

evidence_standards.name: Deterministic simulation evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports 10 initial states per task and 360 rollouts per policy on the 36 held-out tasks. It reports scores but gives no seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, statistical test, or threshold for calling a difference real.

evidence_standards.name: Physical D2S evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Each policy is evaluated over 24 trials at each conveyor speed (72 planned placements per policy–speed condition). The paper reports observed completion fractions; it gives no variance estimates, confidence intervals, statistical test, or significance threshold.

Evaluates 12 challenge categories across 96 settings and 3,296 task-condition cases; each case uses 10 trials with different initial configurations. Reports task success rate. Unless otherwise specified, perturbations affect only visual observations. Recursive predicted-frame feedback is evaluated on LingBot-VA.

metrics.name: Task Success Rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: In target-object and target-receptacle masking, interaction-cue masking, cross-view contradiction, and visual-state ambiguity, high SR can reflect memorized spatial priors, alternative camera views, or non-visual cues rather than genuine visual grounding. The paper interprets these results with controlled comparisons and reports absolute SR drops relative to Normal alongside SR.

controls.name: Normal (clean-observation) condition
controls.detail: Runs the same models and tasks without the visual perturbation; reported alongside perturbed conditions.
controls.rules_out: A change in performance being attributable merely to task or model differences rather than the visual perturbation.

controls.name: Visual State Ambiguity matched comparison
controls.detail: Compared with Task-Precondition Variation on the same receptacle-openness and object-pose attributes; ambiguity weakens visual evidence while preserving the physical state, whereas precondition variation changes the scene.
controls.rules_out: That the performance loss from changed task preconditions is explained simply by difficulty interpreting ambiguous visual evidence.

confounds.name: High success under object masking may reflect learned spatial priors or remaining cues rather than visual grounding
confounds.detail: A policy can succeed despite missing target-object or receptacle appearance by relying on memorized locations or other scene cues.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares target-object and target-receptacle masking with interaction-cue masking and reports the much larger degradation from removing local interaction cues; it interprets high masking SR as potentially reflecting priors and remaining cues, not as proof of visual grounding.

confounds.name: Apparent robustness to distractors may come from following a familiar position rather than identifying the target
confounds.detail: Success rates alone could obscure whether the gripper actually re-localizes the instructed target when a competing object is present.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures trial-level contact composition (target, distractor, both, or neither) and reports increased distractor-only contact when a distractor occupies the target’s familiar position.

confounds.name: Task-precondition failures may be caused by visual uncertainty rather than failure to adapt behavior
confounds.detail: A policy might fail because it cannot interpret the scene, even if it could adapt its action sequence once the state is known.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares precondition changes with visual-state ambiguity on the same openness and pose attributes; ambiguity preserves substantially higher SR while actual precondition changes cause severe degradation.

confounds.name: Simulation failure modes may not transfer to physical manipulation
confounds.detail: The headline simulation vulnerabilities could be specific to the simulated setting.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper runs 200 real-world rollouts on a Franka Research 3 with π₀.₅ and LaWAM across two tasks and four visual perturbations, and reports the corresponding success rates.

evidence_standards.name: 10 trials per simulated task-condition case
evidence_standards.detail: Trials use different initial configurations and results are reported as success rates. The paper does not state confidence intervals, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

evidence_standards.name: 10 trials per real-world task-condition pair
evidence_standards.detail: The paper evaluates two models on two tasks under Normal and four perturbed conditions, totaling 200 physical rollouts; it reports success rates and does not state statistical tests or uncertainty intervals.

metrics.name: Task success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper shows that undocumented evaluation settings can substantially shift success rates (up to 55 percentage points in its examples); it also notes that success rate does not capture subtask progress, efficiency, or safety.

confounds.name: Evaluation-setting mismatches, rather than framework fidelity, explain score discrepancies
confounds.detail: Undocumented preprocessing or action/state conventions can produce large score changes, making a reproduced score gap look like a framework or model failure.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors systematically compared intermediate values with reference implementations and tested the mismatches: using the wrong X-VLA proprioceptive state source changed LIBERO success from 97.8% to 42%; the wrong absolute-versus-delta action mode yielded 0%; the quaternion convention changed OpenVLA-OFT’s LIBERO-Goal score from 97% to 83% and LIBERO-Long from 95% to 56%; omitting OpenVLA’s center crop cost about 3 percentage points.

confounds.name: GR00T’s SimplerEnv score reflects a missing simulator input rather than model performance
confounds.detail: The official SimplerEnv setup lacks the end-effector-pose proprioceptive input GR00T expects, which could make its score appear to be 0%.
confounds.ruled_out_by: After adding the expected pose input through the required simulator patch, the reported reproduction rose from 0% to 59.7%; an 8.0-point gap to the published score remained.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed-seed reproductions compared with published scores
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says validation used fixed seeds and versioned Docker images and reports score deltas against published results. It does not state the seed count for this validation, report a variance estimate, specify a statistical test, or define a numerical margin for treating results as equivalent.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates finetuned VLAs on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long task categories under three inference input settings: vision and language, vision only, and language only. Reports success rates; the paper does not specify a trial count for this evaluation.

datasets.name: LIBERO-CF
datasets.eval_protocol: Four counterfactual suites: CF-Spatial (15 tasks; targets objects originally used as background), CF-Object (10; alternative target objects), CF-Long (10; multi-step instructions with new targets), and CF-OOD (15; objects unseen during finetuning). Runs 50 trials per task across methods. Reports grounding (gripper contacts the instructed target, regardless of task completion) and success (task completion), each split into Faithful (instructed task) and Biased (original training task) behavior.

datasets.name: CF-Focused
datasets.eval_protocol: Focused variant of CF-Spatial, using the same counterfactual instructions but removing training-task objects from the scene. Reports grounding and success rates; the paper does not separately state its trial count.

baselines.name: π₀
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses officially released weights finetuned for LIBERO; simulation comparisons run 50 trials per task across methods.

baselines.fair_comparison: Uses officially released weights finetuned for LIBERO; simulation comparisons run 50 trials per task across methods. In real-world experiments, π₀.₅-DROID is the baseline; the VLA and VA components are fully finetuned for 10k steps with batch size 32.

metrics.name: Grounding rate
metrics.caveat: Measures contact with the instructed target regardless of task completion, so it does not establish task execution; the paper reports success rate alongside it.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper describes it as a stricter measure of task execution than grounding; it reports grounding rate alongside it.

metrics.name: Faithful
metrics.caveat: Indicates following the instructed task; the paper also reports Biased behavior, which indicates following the original training task.

metrics.name: Biased
metrics.caveat: Indicates following the original training task instead of the counterfactual instruction; the paper reports Faithful behavior alongside it.

controls.name: Vanilla VLA without CAG (R1)
controls.detail: The unmodified π₀.₅ baseline, compared with CAG strategies in the training-strategy ablation.
controls.rules_out: That the CAG results are simply the baseline performance without guidance.

controls.name: Random-language-dropout VLA used as both branches (R2)
controls.detail: A VLA finetuned with random language dropout is used as both the conditional and unconditional policies.
controls.rules_out: That language-dropout training alone provides the same benefit as the paper's CAG strategies.

controls.name: Inference modality ablations
controls.detail: For each finetuned VLA on LIBERO, the paper evaluates standard vision-and-language inputs, vision-only inputs, and language-only inputs.
controls.rules_out: Whether the observed performance depends on language input or can be maintained from vision alone.

controls.name: CF-Spatial with training-task objects removed (CF-Focused)
controls.detail: The same counterfactual instructions are evaluated after removing training-task objects from the scene.
controls.rules_out: Whether the training-task objects in the scene contribute to the observed counterfactual behavior.

confounds.name: CAG gains could come at the cost of performance on the original in-domain tasks
confounds.detail: A headline improvement on under-observed counterfactual tasks could look beneficial even if guidance damages the model's well-learned task performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that real-world CAG improvements on under-observed tasks come without loss on the original training tasks.

evidence_standards.name: Simulation run count
evidence_standards.detail: Runs 50 trials per task across all methods on LIBERO-CF; the paper does not state statistical tests, confidence intervals, or variance reporting.

evidence_standards.name: Real-world run count
evidence_standards.detail: Runs 10 trials per instruction; the paper does not state statistical tests, confidence intervals, or variance reporting.

metrics.name: ASR_u (Untargeted Attack Success Rate)
metrics.caveat: For attacks intended to disrupt task completion, failures can reflect the model's inherent limitations rather than the attack; the paper reports clean performance alongside backdoor results and acknowledges attribution remains difficult.

metrics.name: ASR_t (Targeted Attack Success Rate)
metrics.caveat: Uses a strict criterion: the model must reproduce the predefined long-horizon action sequence; the paper notes results are inherently influenced by the target VLA's capabilities. Clean performance is also reported for backdoor attacks.

metrics.name: Task success rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that low clean task performance can make ASR_u failures difficult to attribute to the attack; ASR_u is defined as 1 − SR.

controls.name: Trigger-free clean inputs
controls.detail: Backdoor models are evaluated on inputs without the trigger to measure clean performance.
controls.rules_out: That the backdoor result merely reflects degradation of normal task performance; the paper reports clean performance alongside backdoor attack success.

controls.name: Visual-only and textual-only trigger ablations
controls.detail: BackdoorVLA is evaluated with visual-only, textual-only, and bi-modal triggers.
controls.rules_out: That the reported bi-modal result requires both modalities, or that adding a modality necessarily improves attack performance.

confounds.name: Untargeted failures reflect the VLA's inherent task limitations rather than the attack
confounds.detail: A failed task—and hence a high ASR_u—could occur even without the attack, producing the same headline result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper additionally evaluates clean performance on trigger-free inputs for backdoor methods, but explicitly says this makes attribution difficult and calls for more refined evaluation; it does not claim the concern is fully resolved.

confounds.name: Targeted success differences reflect the target VLA's inherent capabilities rather than backdoor effectiveness alone
confounds.detail: The strict ASR_t requires reproducing a predefined long-horizon sequence, so model capability can affect the headline score independently of the backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports clean performance alongside backdoor results, but explicitly notes that ASR_t is inherently influenced by the target VLA's capabilities; it reports no measurement that fully separates these effects.

evidence_standards.name: 200 real-world trials
evidence_standards.detail: All real-world evaluations are conducted over 200 trials. The paper does not state simulation trial counts, seeds, variance summaries, statistical tests, or a threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites; reports success rate (%) averaged within each suite and across suites, using 50 held-out test scenes or randomized initial conditions per task. Uses single-view images; robot proprioceptive states are excluded for LIBERO.

baselines.name: OpenVLA-OFT
baselines.fair_comparison: VLA-Thinker is initialized from publicly available OpenVLA-OFT weights. The paper notes differing inputs: VLA-Thinker uses single-view images, while official OpenVLA-OFT also uses wrist-camera images; LIBERO runs omit proprioceptive states.

controls.name: OpenVLA-OFT reference model
controls.detail: The end-to-end policy predicts actions without explicit intermediate reasoning; compared with VLA-Thinker on LIBERO.
controls.rules_out: A gain attributable only to comparing against another reasoning-enabled model; the comparison tests VLA-Thinker against a direct-action reference.

controls.name: VLA-Thinker-SFT
controls.detail: Ablation trained with SFT cold-start only, without GRPO.
controls.rules_out: That the full model's result is explained by SFT alone; the paper reports 95.0% average LIBERO success for this variant versus 97.5% for the full model.

controls.name: VLA-Thinker-GRPO
controls.detail: Ablation trained with GRPO only, without SFT initialization.
controls.rules_out: That GRPO without the cold-start stage is sufficient; the paper reports 88.2% average LIBERO success for this variant versus 97.5% for the full model.

confounds.name: The full-model gain comes from SFT alone rather than the combined training pipeline
confounds.detail: If structured CoT supervision alone explained the headline result, adding trajectory-level GRPO would not be needed to obtain it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the full model with the SFT-only ablation on LIBERO: 97.5% versus 95.0% average success.

confounds.name: GRPO alone accounts for the result, without a need for SFT initialization
confounds.detail: If sparse-reward GRPO by itself explained the headline result, omitting the cold-start stage would not substantially reduce performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the full model with the GRPO-only ablation on LIBERO: 97.5% versus 88.2% average success.

datasets.name: LIBERO

metrics.name: Task success rate
metrics.caveat: Suite success rates can reflect each suite’s baseline fragility rather than the patch’s specific effect; the paper also measures the success-rate drop relative to a random patch. Lower success rate indicates a stronger attack.

Average L2 distance between clean and patched decoded actions

controls.name: Random patch
controls.detail: Random noise in [0,1] with identical size and position to the adversarial patch.
controls.rules_out: That generic random perturbation of the same size and position explains the attack result.

controls.name: Blank patch
controls.detail: A uniform mid-grey patch used to isolate occlusion.
controls.rules_out: That occlusion alone explains the attack result.

controls.name: No attack
controls.detail: Evaluates the model without an adversarial patch.
controls.rules_out: Provides the unmodified reference for the observed success-rate change.

controls.name: Single-term loss ablations
controls.detail: Tests individual terms of the VIS and IGS losses and compares them with the corresponding combined loss on OpenVLA-LIBERO-Spatial.
controls.rules_out: That the combined loss’s effect is attributable to only one of its component terms.

controls.name: VIS-only and IGS-only attacks
controls.detail: Compares each objective alone with the joint attack.
controls.rules_out: That the joint attack’s result is explained by just one of the two objectives.

confounds.name: The attack effect is generic patch damage or occlusion, not the proposed optimized attack
confounds.detail: A random patch or a blank patch could lower task success without the proposed ancestor-VLM objectives being effective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against random noise with identical size and position and against a uniform mid-grey patch; the paper reports lower success rates for its attacks.

confounds.name: Differences across LIBERO suites reflect baseline fragility rather than task-specific attack effect
confounds.detail: A suite with lower baseline robustness could show a larger apparent attack effect even if the patch is not especially effective for its tasks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure success-rate drop relative to a random patch for each suite.

confounds.name: Ours-IGS performs better when optimized on BridgeData V2 only because that dataset is larger
confounds.detail: The BridgeData V2 advantage could be due to having more optimization data rather than its broader scene and task coverage.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Re-optimize Ours-IGS on a BridgeData V2 subset the same size as the LIBERO set and compare its LIBERO success rates with patches optimized on LIBERO and on the full BridgeData V2 set.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds; report the mean
evidence_standards.detail: The paper optimizes five patches with different random seeds and reports mean task success rate; it does not state confidence intervals or a statistical significance test.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites (10 tasks per suite); runs 50 rollouts per task, for 500 trials per suite. Uses the maximum number of steps in the training data as the timeout. Reports Success Rate (SR) and Failure Rate (FR = 1 - SR).

controls.name: Clean
controls.detail: Evaluates the unperturbed model on LIBERO.
controls.rules_out: That the attack results merely reflect the model's baseline task failures.

controls.name: Random Noise
controls.detail: Applies uniform random noise; the paper reports results across perturbation bounds, including comparisons at the corresponding noise constraint.
controls.rules_out: That uniform random perturbation alone explains the attack's increased failure rate.

controls.name: ADVLA without attention-guided strategies
controls.detail: The base ADVLA feature-space attack, compared with ADVLA-AW, ADVLA-TKM, and ADVLA-TKL.
controls.rules_out: For the attention-guided variants, that their results are explained solely by using the underlying feature-space attack.

confounds.name: Uniform random perturbations alone cause the increased failure rate
confounds.detail: The attack's higher failure rates could result from adding noise, rather than from its feature-space attack procedure or attention-guided strategies.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports LIBERO failure rates for Random Noise alongside the attack methods, including under the reported perturbation constraints.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with RT-2-X on the Google Robot evaluations; both are 55B and web-pretrained. RT-2 uses Google Robot action data, while RT-2-X uses the robotics data mixture.

controls.name: RT-2-X trained without Bridge
controls.detail: Uses the RT-2-X training data except for Bridge; evaluated on the Google Robot emergent-skills tasks.
controls.rules_out: That the emergent-skills result is unchanged when Bridge data is removed; the reduction in performance supports a role for Bridge/WidowX data.

controls.name: RT-2-X without web pretraining
controls.detail: A 5B RT-2-X model trained from scratch, compared with a web-pretrained 5B RT-2-X model with history.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance in this comparison can be achieved without web pretraining.

controls.name: RT-2-X without image history
controls.detail: A 5B RT-2-X model with no history, compared with a 5B model using a history of two images.
controls.rules_out: That the observed generalization difference is independent of the image-history input.

controls.name: RT-2
controls.detail: The 55B web-pretrained model using Google Robot action data, compared with 55B web-pretrained RT-2-X on the Google Robot evaluations.
controls.rules_out: That RT-2-X's results are simply the performance of the web-pretrained RT-2 model without the X-embodiment robotics data.

confounds.name: The gains reflect model capacity rather than X-embodiment training
confounds.detail: A larger model could perform better regardless of whether it benefits from multi-robot data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares RT-2-X with RT-2 at the same 55B size and notes that RT-1-X and RT-1 have the same architecture; it also reports a 5B versus 55B RT-2-X ablation.

confounds.name: Emergent-skill gains do not depend on transfer from Bridge/WidowX data
confounds.detail: The Google Robot gains could arise from other parts of RT-2-X training rather than the Bridge skills collected on another robot.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Removing Bridge from RT-2-X training reduces performance on the held-out emergent-skills tasks.

Conditions are paired at the same episode boundary with the same remaining step budget; an episode is counted at a duration only when every compared branch has a valid state there (n decreases from 77 at t* to 69 at t*+5). Uses the center crop prescribed for the released LIBERO checkpoints. Recovery-method evaluation uses three initial states per task at each activation latency; held-out-patch results use 26 eligible recovery episodes per run and clean success over 30 episodes.

Uses the center crop prescribed for the released LIBERO checkpoints. Recovery-method evaluation uses three initial states per task at each activation latency; held-out-patch results use 28 eligible recovery episodes per run and clean success over 30 episodes.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the matched training budget: same base checkpoint, number of training frames, optimization steps, and three training seeds.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the matched training budget: same base checkpoint, number of training frames, optimization steps, and three training seeds; it uses attack-induced states collected only at the shortest duration.

metrics.name: Post-removal recovery rate
metrics.caveat: Continuous-attack task success does not characterize recoverability after patch removal; the paper instead resumes the frozen policy from matched states with the patch removed and the same remaining step budget.

metrics.name: Task success rate under continuous attack
metrics.caveat: It measures performance while the perturbation remains present and does not characterize recoverability after patch removal; the paper also reports post-removal recovery.

metrics.name: Action deviation magnitude
metrics.caveat: Per-step action deviation characterizes the policy while perturbed but does not measure what happens after patch removal; the paper additionally measures post-removal recovery.

metrics.name: Adversarial excess
metrics.caveat: The paper defines it as a difference between recovery success rates and reports it, with confidence intervals, in percentage points.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity between consecutive deviation vectors
Steps in contact with the scene

controls.name: Clean branch
controls.detail: A clean trajectory for the same episode, resumed at the same boundary and evaluated with the same remaining step budget.
controls.rules_out: That lower recovery in the adversarial branch is explained by a shorter remaining horizon.

controls.name: Random-patch control
controls.detail: A random-content patch with the adversarial patch's support and location; the attack configuration uses the same patch size and anchor.
controls.rules_out: That the recovery gap is explained by visual occlusion alone.

controls.name: Deviation-matched control
controls.detail: At each boundary, adds an independently sampled random action direction scaled to match the adversarial action-deviation magnitude.
controls.rules_out: That the recovery gap is explained by action-error magnitude alone.

controls.name: Fixed-direction control
controls.detail: Matches the adversarial action-deviation magnitude boundary by boundary and reuses one sampled direction throughout each episode.
controls.rules_out: That the recovery gap is explained by action-error magnitude combined with persistent directional deviation.

controls.name: No-defense policy
controls.detail: The original frozen policy without the recovery adapter.
controls.rules_out: Provides the untreated reference for whether an intervention improves recovery.

controls.name: Image augmentation
controls.detail: Training uses photometric corruption on clean expert states, under the matched optimization budget.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether recovery gains follow from ordinary image augmentation rather than training on adversarial observations.

controls.name: Recovery (single duration)
controls.detail: A recovery ablation trained on attack-induced states collected only at the shortest duration.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the multi-duration state collection in the paper's adapter is necessary for its recovery results.

confounds.name: The apparent persistent effect is caused by visual occlusion
confounds.detail: A lower recovery rate after the adversarial trajectory could result from the patch obscuring the image rather than adversarial optimization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with a random-content patch matched in support and location; report the post-removal recovery contrast against this control.

confounds.name: The apparent persistent effect is caused by larger action errors
confounds.detail: The adversarial branch may simply accumulate larger action deviations than a non-adversarial perturbation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a control that matches adversarial action-deviation magnitude at every boundary and compare post-removal recovery.

confounds.name: The apparent persistent effect is caused by temporally persistent action direction
confounds.detail: Coherent deviations over time could reduce recoverability without an adversarial-specific effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use a fixed-direction control that matches deviation magnitude and imposes persistent direction; its recovery remains higher than the adversarial branch.

confounds.name: Different remaining time explains the recovery gap
confounds.detail: Branches resumed later could have less time to complete the task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Resume all conditions at the same episode boundary with an identical remaining step budget; the clean branch retains 100% recovery in the reported paired episodes.

confounds.name: The recovery gap reflects irreversible scene changes
confounds.detail: Adversarial actions might alter the environment so that task completion is no longer possible, rather than leave a less favorable state under the available horizon.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report that no object leaves the workspace and that observed failures exhaust the step budget rather than terminate through simulator failure; also report contact-step counts by condition.

confounds.name: State-restoration errors cause branch differences
confounds.detail: A resumed rollout could diverge from its source because the simulator snapshot omits state needed to reproduce execution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Validate replay consistency: the action sequence, termination step, and task outcome must match the original continuation before using a checkpoint.

confounds.name: Ordinary occlusion spuriously determines attack onset
confounds.detail: A patch could appear to have an onset merely because it changes action predictions through generic visual occlusion.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Calibrate the onset threshold using the 95th percentile of matched random-patch deviations and require two consecutive threshold crossings.

confounds.name: Recovery gains arise from fitting the training patches rather than generalizing
confounds.detail: The adapter could benefit from seeing the same patches during training and evaluation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate with held-out patches optimized on disjoint trajectories and with different random seeds.

confounds.name: Recovery gains come with degraded nominal task performance
confounds.detail: An intervention might improve attacked-state recovery by damaging ordinary clean behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report clean-task success alongside recovery; the paper reports it as comparable to the undefended policy, with no clear reduction.

evidence_standards.name: Paired 95% confidence intervals for recovery comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Comparisons are paired by task, initial state, random seed, and patch anchor; confidence intervals are computed by paired bootstrap resampling stratified by task. Adversarial excess and its interval are reported in percentage points.

evidence_standards.name: Three training seeds
evidence_standards.detail: All trained methods use three training seeds. Table III reports values with ± for trained-method results, but the excerpt does not specify what the ± quantity represents.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the goal, spatial, long (10), and object sections; 100 episodes per section (400 total, 66,931 steps across the evaluated checkpoints and fine-tunes). Probes are trained with a train/validation/test split and evaluated on each section’s test set; split proportions are not specified. Evaluates horizons K=1, 3, 10, and 30 using R² on state-transition embedding vectors. Embeddings are mean-pooled across token positions.

baselines.name: Probes trained on raw embeddings
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with activation-based probes for the same dataset, layer, horizon, and probe type; the reported comparison uses the highest R² among linear and MLP probes for each condition.

metrics.name: R²
metrics.caveat: Predicting the future embedding directly could be trivial because it is similar to the current embedding; the paper instead predicts the future-minus-current embedding transition vector.

controls.name: Probes trained on raw embeddings
controls.detail: Train probes on the embeddings rather than internal activations to compare against what the probe can predict without the model’s internal computations.
controls.rules_out: If activation-based probes outperform this condition, the result is less readily explained by the probe learning the transition from raw embeddings alone.

confounds.name: The probe learns the state transition from its inputs rather than revealing a representation in OpenVLA’s internal computations
confounds.detail: Probe performance could reflect the probe’s own predictive ability over the inputs, rather than latent transition information computed by the model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train probes on raw embeddings as a baseline and test whether activation-based probe R² exceeds embedding-based probe R²; the paper reports one-way statistical tests and that activations uniformly exceed embeddings.

evidence_standards.name: Moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Confidence intervals are calculated across 400 moving-block bootstrap R² replicates, with automatic block length b=max(2, floor(n^(1/3))) and Bessel’s correction; standard error across replicates is reported.

evidence_standards.name: Permutation tests
evidence_standards.detail: Uses 100 random label shuffles for p-values, tests only probes with positive R², and retains hyperparameters from the original dataset rather than retuning per permutation. Reports successful tests at p<0.01 and overall p<0.0001 across 123 OpenVLA probes.

evidence_standards.name: MLP-versus-linear probe comparison
evidence_standards.detail: Uses a two-way statistical comparison and reports 90%, 95%, and 99% two-sided confidence-interval results; MLP probes are not significantly higher in R² than linear probes.

datasets.name: BridgeData V2
datasets.eval_protocol: Out-of-the-box WidowX evaluation: 17 tasks, 10 trials per task (170 rollouts per approach), scored by success rate; comparisons use the same tasks and initial robot/object states. The final model uses 224×224 px inputs. Additional evaluations: five language-grounding tasks in the sink environment for backbone comparisons; eight representative tasks and 80 rollouts per approach for quantization.

datasets.name: Google robot evaluations
datasets.eval_protocol: Out-of-the-box evaluation on 12 tasks, 5 trials per task (60 rollouts per approach), scored by success rate; comparisons use the same tasks and initial robot/object states.

datasets.name: Franka-Tabletop
