The parameter-efficient fine-tuning comparison uses select tasks and 33 rollouts per approach. Scored by success rate.

datasets.name: Franka-DROID
datasets.eval_protocol: Fine-tuning evaluation among seven Franka tasks using 10–150 demonstrations per task; the overall fine-tuning comparison reports 30 rollouts on Franka-DROID tasks. Scored by success rate.

baselines.name: RT-1-X
baselines.fair_comparison: Out-of-the-box comparisons use the same evaluation tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA.

baselines.name: RT-2-X
baselines.fair_comparison: Out-of-the-box comparisons use the same evaluation tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA.

baselines.name: Octo
baselines.fair_comparison: Out-of-the-box comparisons use the same evaluation tasks and initial robot/object states as OpenVLA; for downstream fine-tuning, Octo is fine-tuned on the target dataset.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy
baselines.fair_comparison: Trained from scratch on the downstream task demonstrations; the paper notes that this version uses observation history, proprioception, action chunking, and absolute Cartesian actions, unlike the other compared policies.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy (matched)
baselines.fair_comparison: Configured to match OpenVLA’s input/output specifications: a single image, no proprioception or observation history, and one relative-position action without action chunking.

baselines.name: IDEFICS-1
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with LLaVA on BridgeData V2 tasks; the paper does not specify further matching conditions.

baselines.name: LLaVA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with IDEFICS-1 on BridgeData V2 tasks; the paper does not specify further matching conditions.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: For 8-bit quantized inference, the reported success-rate drop may reflect reduced inference speed and changed system dynamics rather than poorer action prediction; the paper also reports offline token accuracy and control frequency.

metrics.name: Inference speed / control frequency
metrics.caveat: Inference speed can affect real-world success by changing system dynamics relative to data collection; the paper reports rollout performance alongside speed.

controls.name: OpenVLA (scratch)
controls.detail: Fine-tune the underlying Prismatic VLM on the target robot setup rather than fine-tuning the OpenX-pretrained OpenVLA model.
controls.rules_out: Whether downstream performance depends on OpenX robot pretraining rather than only fine-tuning the base VLM on target-task data.

controls.name: Last layer only
controls.detail: Fine-tune only the last transformer layer and token embedding matrix.
controls.rules_out: Whether updating the full model is necessary for the reported fine-tuning performance.

controls.name: Frozen vision
controls.detail: Freeze the vision encoder while fine-tuning the other weights.
controls.rules_out: Whether adapting the vision encoder is necessary for the reported fine-tuning performance.

controls.name: bfloat16 inference
controls.detail: Use the default, unquantized inference precision as the reference for int8 and int4 quantized inference.
controls.rules_out: Whether quantized-inference memory and performance results differ from the default precision model.

confounds.name: Quantized-model performance loss is due to reduced inference speed rather than degraded action prediction
confounds.detail: The 8-bit model performs worse in real-world rollouts, which could otherwise be attributed to quantization reducing prediction accuracy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Offline token accuracy is reported as comparable for int8, int4, and bfloat16; the paper also reports that int8 runs at 1.2 Hz and changes system dynamics, while int4 runs at 3 Hz and has similar rollout performance to bfloat16.

confounds.name: OpenVLA’s gains over RT-2-X may reflect training-data and vision-encoder differences rather than the model comparison alone
confounds.detail: The paper identifies OpenVLA’s larger training mixture, additional data cleaning, and fused spatial/semantic vision encoder as factors that may explain the performance difference.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper points to ablation analyses of these components in Appendix D; the supplied text does not give their specific measurements or results.

evidence_standards.name: Reported rollout variability and paired A/B comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Success rates are reported as mean ± StdErr, and evaluations use the same tasks and initial robot/object states for A/B comparisons. No statistical test, significance threshold, or rule for calling a difference real is specified.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Four standard suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long/"10"), 10 tasks per suite; 50 episodes per task (2,000 rollouts total), fixed evaluation seed and hard environment resets. Reports success rate by suite and four-suite average. Ablation screens use 25 episodes per task where noted, with conclusions re-confirmed at 50. Evaluation uses center-cropped 128×128 images; the paper reports no held-out task split.

datasets.name: LIBERO-90
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates 89 tasks (one of the 90 has no demonstrations), 10 episodes per task, single seed; reports average success. Evaluation is pinned to the renderer version matching the dataset’s scenes. Task IDs index distinct instruction strings, so some tasks share an ID.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Plus
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates a stratified sample of perturbations across 40 tasks and 7 factors; 2 episodes per variant, with identical variants for each model. Reports success by perturbation factor and average. Rephrased instructions are mapped to the corresponding base-task ID; visually identical language variants serve as the unperturbed baseline.

baselines.name: π₀.₅ (LeRobot implementation)
baselines.fair_comparison: The reported success result uses 10 episodes per task (400 rollouts), versus MINERVA’s 50 episodes per task (2,000 rollouts); the paper calls it a reference point rather than a protocol-matched comparison. In the inference-cost table, models are compared on the stated RTX 5080 Laptop GPU / 8 CPU threads, batch 1.

baselines.name: SmolVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared for inference cost on the stated RTX 5080 Laptop GPU / 8 CPU threads, batch 1; the paper describes the hardware as identical.

baselines.name: BID-style candidate selection
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same 0.54M checkpoint and inference-strategy protocol; the strategy screen uses 25 episodes per task. BID selects the most coherent of 16 sampled chunks.

baselines.name: RTC-style soft inpainting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same 0.54M checkpoint and inference-strategy protocol; the strategy screen uses 25 episodes per task.

baselines.name: Plain chunking
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared using the same 0.54M checkpoint and inference-strategy protocol; the strategy screen uses 25 episodes per task.

metrics.name: Success rate (per suite and four-suite average)
metrics.caveat: The paper says standard LIBERO success can conceal that the benchmark primarily measures task-indexed memorization rather than generalization. It reports LIBERO-Plus perturbation success alongside standard LIBERO results to measure robustness beyond the standard score.

metrics.name: Inference time per action chunk (GPU/CPU wall-clock latency)

controls.name: Within-suite task-ID permutation
controls.detail: On the released 1M checkpoint, all weights are fixed and task IDs are rotated within each suite.
controls.rules_out: A result attributable only to correlation between task identity and success; the collapse tests whether the task-ID mapping itself selects the executed task.

controls.name: Force every task to its suite’s task-0 ID
controls.detail: On the same fixed 1M checkpoint, replace each task’s ID with the suite’s task-0 ID.
controls.rules_out: That the original task-ID conditioning is unnecessary for task selection; the resulting near-chance performance is compared with the correctly mapped condition.

controls.name: LIBERO-Plus language variants
controls.detail: Visually identical to base scenes and used as the unperturbed baseline in the perturbation evaluation; identical variants are evaluated across models.
controls.rules_out: That the perturbation-related score drop is merely a renderer artifact rather than an effect of the perturbations.

confounds.name: Standard-LIBERO success reflects memorization rather than general capability
confounds.detail: The headline score could remain high because the policy selects among memorized tasks in the same scenes, without demonstrating open-vocabulary understanding or robustness to changed conditions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates LIBERO-Plus perturbations and reports success by factor; scores fall substantially, with near-zero success on photometric shifts. This measures and delimits the limitation rather than establishing generalization.

confounds.name: Task-ID conditioning is correlated with success but does not causally select the task
confounds.detail: The high standard-LIBERO score could arise from visual context or other learned behavior even if the task-ID mapping were not doing the claimed task-selection work.
confounds.ruled_out_by: With weights fixed, rotate task IDs within each suite or force all tasks to the suite’s task-0 ID; success collapses from 96.75% to 6.5% or 16.2%, respectively.

confounds.name: LIBERO-Plus score loss is a renderer artifact
confounds.detail: The lower perturbed-scene score could reflect an evaluation-renderer difference rather than sensitivity to perturbations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Language variants are visually identical to base scenes and serve as the unperturbed baseline; they lose approximately zero points.

confounds.name: Small ablation differences are training-seed noise
confounds.detail: A single-run gain or loss around one point could arise from seed-to-seed variation rather than the tested design choice.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The key ablation configurations are retrained with three seeds and reported as mean ± standard deviation; the baseline spans 94.60–96.75%, establishing an approximately ±1-point seed band used to interpret differences.

evidence_standards.name: Three training seeds for key ablations; mean ± standard deviation and an approximately ±1-point seed band
evidence_standards.detail: The paper treats differences within the observed seed band as no detectable difference; it reports no formal statistical test. Headline models and many other sweep points are single runs, and evaluation uses one fixed simulator evaluation seed.

evidence_standards.name: Reported inference results use a specified execution and decoding setup
evidence_standards.detail: The policy replans every control step and uses ACT-style temporal ensembling with decay 0.01 per step of age; sub-1M flow models use initial-noise temperature 0.85. The inference-strategy screen uses 25 episodes per task, and the selected strategy is re-confirmed at 50 episodes per task.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Goal
datasets.eval_protocol: Canonical-instruction reference condition; tasks start from identical initial states. Compared using binary task success rate. Episode count and split details are not stated.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Para
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates held-out paraphrases while keeping other factors fixed, independently varying action and object expressions and including compositional variations. Approximately 100 samples per variation type, 4,092 paraphrased instructions total. Reports binary success rate and PRIDE; PRIDE uses α=0.5 by default. Episode count is not stated.

datasets.name: CALVIN-Para
datasets.eval_protocol: Applies the same two-axis paraphrase design to CALVIN and evaluates two CALVIN-native VLAs. Reports success rate, PRIDE, and planning-level failure proportions. Split and episode counts are not stated.

baselines.name: OpenVLA-OFTgoal
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with OpenVLA-OFTmixed within the same architecture and simulator; OFTmixed uses four times the task-level data diversity.

baselines.name: OpenVLA-OFTmixed
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with OpenVLA-OFTgoal within the same architecture and simulator; OFTmixed uses four times the task-level data diversity.

baselines.name: π 0.5
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the expert-only variant; the standard model jointly fine-tunes the VLM and Action Expert, while the variant freezes the VLM and fine-tunes only the Action Expert.

baselines.name: π 0.5 (expert-only)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with standard π 0.5; this variant freezes the VLM and fine-tunes only the Action Expert.

baselines.name: RoboFlamingo
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated as a CALVIN-native VLA on CALVIN-Para; no additional matching conditions are stated.

baselines.name: FLOWER
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated as a CALVIN-native VLA on CALVIN-Para; no additional matching conditions are stated.

metrics.name: Success rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Binary SR treats all paraphrases equally and can obscure whether success is limited to easier variations; the paper reports PRIDE alongside it.

metrics.name: Overestimation
metrics.caveat: Defined as (SR − PRIDE) / SR to quantify how much uniform SR overstates paraphrase robustness; reported alongside SR and PRIDE.

metrics.name: Far-GT percentage
metrics.caveat: Classifies failures as planning-level when their trajectory DTW distance from the mean successful trajectory exceeds τ; Near-GT failures are reported alongside it.

metrics.name: Near-GT percentage
metrics.caveat: Classifies failures as execution-level when their trajectory DTW distance from the mean successful trajectory is within τ; Far-GT failures are reported alongside it.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation with SR
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that the correlation can be confounded by a model with low base-task performance; it also reports rankings across the seven VLAs.

metrics.name: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) distance
metrics.caveat: Used to classify failures relative to the mean successful trajectory, with τ set to the maximum DTW distance among successful episodes.

controls.name: Original canonical instructions (None × None / LIBERO-Goal)
controls.detail: Evaluated alongside paraphrased instructions; the benchmark keeps other factors fixed, and LIBERO-Goal tasks begin from identical initial states.
controls.rules_out: A performance drop attributable simply to the task or scene rather than to changing the instruction phrasing.

confounds.name: Paraphrase fragility is specific to an architecture or model scale
confounds.detail: The degradation could reflect a weakness of one architecture family or scale rather than a broader VLA vulnerability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates seven configurations across four architecture families and scales and reports degradation across all of them.

confounds.name: More diverse fine-tuning data explains or removes the paraphrase gap
confounds.detail: The headline drop could be due to limited task diversity in fine-tuning, rather than robustness to linguistic variation itself.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares OpenVLA-OFTgoal with OpenVLA-OFTmixed, which has four times the task-level data diversity, and reports similar drops.

confounds.name: The fine-tuning strategy explains the paraphrase gap
confounds.detail: The drop could be caused by whether the VLM is adapted, rather than by paraphrasing as such.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares jointly fine-tuned π 0.5 with the variant that freezes the VLM and fine-tunes only the Action Expert; both still show substantial paraphrase drops.

confounds.name: Failures reflect execution errors rather than incorrect task identification or planning
confounds.detail: A model could identify the intended task but fail while executing the correct trajectory, producing the same binary failure result.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Classifies failures using DTW distance to the mean successful trajectory, with the threshold set to the maximum distance among successful episodes; reports Near-GT and Far-GT proportions.

confounds.name: The object-axis degradation is actually due to action variation
confounds.detail: The observed paraphrase degradation could be driven by action phrasing rather than object-reference changes.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Separately compares object-preserved and object-paraphrased conditions and analyzes the action and object axes independently; reports larger drops for object paraphrasing.

datasets.name: PhAIL
datasets.eval_protocol: Real-robot bin-to-bin pick-and-place on a Franka FR3 with four objects (wooden spoons, towels, scissors, batteries). Each rollout has a 30 s/item cap; analyses use about 995 episodes total, including 396 human-reference episodes, with 32–46 episodes per cell for OpenPI, GR00T, and ACT and 26–34 for SmolVLA. Successful placements yield inter-success times; timeouts are right-censored, and specified unrecoverable failures are represented as T=∞. CDFs are estimated with Kaplan–Meier; HRT and KS are macro-averaged equally across objects. RMST/HRT use τ=240 s, except the sample-efficiency experiment, which uses τ=120 s for RMST and KS. No train/test evaluation split is specified.

baselines.name: OpenPI π0.5
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same four objects, fixture, and evaluation protocol as the other VLAs; all VLAs were fine-tuned on the same 449-episode demonstration set using their repositories’ default recipes, with no per-model hyperparameter search.

baselines.name: GR00T N1.6
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same four objects, fixture, and evaluation protocol as the other VLAs; all VLAs were fine-tuned on the same 449-episode demonstration set using their repositories’ default recipes, with no per-model hyperparameter search.

baselines.name: ACT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same four objects, fixture, and evaluation protocol as the other VLAs; all VLAs were fine-tuned on the same 449-episode demonstration set using their repositories’ default recipes, with no per-model hyperparameter search.

baselines.name: SmolVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same four objects, fixture, and evaluation protocol as the other VLAs; all VLAs were fine-tuned on the same 449-episode demonstration set using their repositories’ default recipes, with no per-model hyperparameter search.

baselines.name: Human reference (teleoperation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Same fixture and hardware as the VLAs; used as the per-object reference for HRT. The paper reports 396 human-reference rollouts; policy and human scenes were not replayed as matched configurations.

metrics.name: Time-to-success CDF
metrics.caveat: A scalar projection discards distributional information, and crossing CDFs can produce opposite rankings under different scalars; the paper reports CDFs and uses scalar summaries alongside them.

metrics.name: Human-Relative Throughput (HRT)
metrics.caveat: The scalar ranking can differ from other principled summaries of the same CDF; it is capped at τ=240 s and excludes reset, recovery, and intervention time outside the per-operation envelope. The paper reports RMST and AUC-versus-human results alongside HRT.

metrics.name: RMST
metrics.caveat: The integration cap can change rankings, and RMST can disagree with other CDF summaries when curves cross; the paper also reports HRT, AUC-versus-human, and CDF-level comparisons.

metrics.name: Success rate at threshold F(τ)
metrics.caveat: A threshold hides distributional differences outside that time point; F(30 s) and F(60 s) did not reach 80% detection on any close pair within N≤30. The paper compares these with macro-KS and reports CDFs.

metrics.name: Macro-averaged Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic (KS)
metrics.caveat: KS tests whether distributions differ but does not provide a coherent direction or ranking; the paper uses macro RMST difference for direction and reports logrank as a sanity check.

metrics.name: Logrank test
metrics.caveat: The paper uses it as a sanity check alongside its per-object macro-KS test; the reported model-pair p-values are Bonferroni-corrected over six pairs.

metrics.name: AUC versus human reference
metrics.caveat: Because the human reference is much faster, the AUC integral is concentrated on the short-time region and can rank policies differently from integrated RMST/HRT; the paper reports HRT/RMST alongside it.

metrics.name: Intervention rate
metrics.caveat: It is a lower bound because drops outside the workspace are not included; the paper reports it alongside the other headline results.

metrics.name: Detection rate
metrics.caveat: It depends on the tested sample size and significance threshold; the paper reports detection rates across 300 outer subsampling trials, with p<0.05 as detection and 80% as the target.

confounds.name: Object difficulty could distort cross-policy comparisons
confounds.detail: Objects differ in difficulty, so aggregate operation counts or pooled comparisons could obscure or distort policy differences.
confounds.ruled_out_by: HRT is normalized within each object against that object’s human reference and then macro-averaged with equal object weights; KS is also computed per object and macro-averaged. The authors note that HRT’s difficulty cancellation is approximate.

confounds.name: Spatial-configuration shifts could explain apparent policy differences
confounds.detail: The paper reports that a same-side versus opposite-side camera/tote configuration shift changes GR00T’s completion rate by 22 percentage points, larger than the GR00T–OpenPI gap.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The evaluation uses a blinded operator and a scheduler that randomly selects which model runs next on the same fixture. The paper recommends blinded, randomized same-session rotation; it also notes that scenes are not replayed between policies, so configurations are not matched.

confounds.name: Annotation bias could affect event timestamps or rankings
confounds.detail: About 40% of episodes required manual review, performed by a single non-blinded reviewer; the authors say annotator bias is not directly controlled.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that the ranking is robust to the label-stream subset used and is the same on the manually reviewed cohort alone. It notes that logged operator counts determine success counts, while manual review supplies per-item timestamps.

confounds.name: Differences in fine-tuning recipes could contribute to model rankings
confounds.detail: Each model uses its repository’s default recipe, and per-model recipe optimization could shift the rankings.
confounds.ruled_out_by: All VLAs use the same 449-episode demonstration set, but the paper does not test optimized or matched hyperparameters; it explicitly leaves this explanation unresolved.

evidence_standards.name: 95% episode-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals
evidence_standards.detail: Scoring scalars and CDF curves use 95% intervals; scalar intervals use 1,000 bootstrap resamples of whole episodes, not individual operations, because operations within an episode are correlated. The paper reports seed 0 only.

evidence_standards.name: Pooled-resample episode-clustered bootstrap for KS p-values
evidence_standards.detail: Under the null, episodes are pooled per object and resampled with replacement into arms of the original sizes. The main analysis reports p-values; the logrank sanity-check p-values are Bonferroni-corrected over six model pairs.

evidence_standards.name: Detection-rate experiment
evidence_standards.detail: For each tested sample size, 300 outer subsampling trials are run with replacement and a 200-replicate inner episode-clustered bootstrap. A trial counts as detected at p<0.05; 80% detection is the stated power target.

evidence_standards.name: Single reported seed
evidence_standards.detail: The results section states that all reported numbers use seed 0; no multi-seed aggregation is reported.

datasets.name: RoboCasa365
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on the Target split with OSMesa rendering, using the four tasks that passed the clean-competence gate: PreSoakPan, RinseSinkBasin, StackBowlsCabinet, and WashLettuce. Each task used 20 fixed base episodes, each run clean and under 12 shifted conditions (four factors × three frozen severity levels), for 1,040 formal rollouts total. Rollouts used the official task horizon and official binary task-success criterion. Clean and perturbed rollouts were paired on task, instruction, scene and object configuration, initial simulator state, horizon, and episode-level policy seed. Shifts were applied one factor at a time: illumination scaling (0.8, 0.6, 0.4); third-person camera yaw/pitch offsets up to 2°, 6°, 10° with wrist view unchanged; robot-base planar-position/yaw offsets (σxy 0.02, 0.05, 0.10 m; σψ 2°, 5°, 10°); or Gaussian blur (σ 1, 2, 4) on policy RGB observations. Severity levels were calibrated and frozen before formal evaluation. Candidate tasks were screened first on 10 clean rollouts, then extended to 20 if they had more than three successes; eligibility required at least 12/20 clean successes.

baselines.name: SmolVLA RoboCasa
baselines.fair_comparison: Screened on the same frozen four-task suite after interface-compatibility and fixed-seed repeatability checks. Clean screening used 10 episodes per task, versus GR00T N1.5's final 20 per task; it did not proceed to perturbation evaluation, so this is not a cross-model robustness comparison.

baselines.name: π0 RoboCasa365 Human300
baselines.fair_comparison: Screened on the same frozen four-task suite after interface-compatibility and fixed-seed repeatability checks. Clean screening used 10 episodes per task, versus GR00T N1.5's final 20 per task; it did not proceed to perturbation evaluation, so this is not a cross-model robustness comparison.

metrics.name: Success rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: Aggregate task success can hide episode-level outcome changes and semantic failure depth; the paper also reports paired outcome transitions and stage-aware diagnostics.

metrics.name: Paired success-rate degradation (ΔSR)
metrics.caveat: Opposing success-to-failure and failure-to-success transitions can cancel, so near-zero ΔSR does not imply episodes were insensitive to the shift; the paper also reports the four paired outcome-transition counts and the number of changed pairs.

metrics.name: Normalized subgoal progress
metrics.caveat: This measures deepest semantic milestone reached, not official task completion; it is reported alongside RoboCasa's official task outcome and first-incomplete-subgoal analysis.

metrics.name: First incomplete subgoal / stage-wise failure distribution
metrics.caveat: It localizes the first unreached semantic milestone but does not identify the causal instant at which failure began; tracker-complete episodes that fail the official criterion are not assigned a first incomplete subgoal.

controls.name: Matched clean rollout
controls.detail: For each perturbed rollout, the clean counterpart shares the task and instruction, scene and object configuration, initial simulator state, horizon, policy, and episode-level policy RNG seed; only the target perturbation differs.
controls.rules_out: Episode-level task-condition differences and uncontrolled policy sampling as explanations for paired clean-versus-shifted outcome changes; the comparison supports attributing observed differences to the evaluated shift under the matched conditions.

confounds.name: Episode difficulty or initial-condition variation explains clean-versus-perturbed differences
confounds.detail: Different episode instances or simulator states could produce different outcomes even without the target shift.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Construct matched clean-perturbed pairs with the same task conditions and initial simulator state; audit pre-shift state fingerprints and rollout metadata.

confounds.name: Policy inference randomness explains paired outcome changes
confounds.detail: Stochastic action sampling could make paired executions differ even if the perturbation had no effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Restore the same checkpoint and RNG state for both rollouts in each pair; the paper validates action-sequence repeatability with shared episode-level seeds.

confounds.name: Low nominal task competence explains perturbation failures
confounds.detail: A policy that often fails on clean tasks could appear non-robust because of baseline task difficulty rather than the shift.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Screen tasks before perturbation evaluation and retain only those with at least 12 successes in 20 clean rollouts.

confounds.name: Perturbation implementation or reset/rendering errors, rather than the intended factor, explain results
confounds.detail: Invalid initialization, pre-shift state mismatch, or unintended changes could produce apparent robustness effects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Run model-free reset/render validity checks before formal evaluation and audit formal rollouts for base-state, seed, renderer, and StageTracker consistency; the reported audits passed.

confounds.name: StageTracker predicates may not represent valid semantic stages
confounds.detail: Stage-aware conclusions could reflect faulty or unrepresentative simulator-state predicates rather than execution progress; the authors also concede these are diagnostics, not ground-truth per-frame stage labels.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Audit the frozen task predicates by replaying five successful target demonstrations per task; all 20 reached milestones in order without predicate errors. The paper notes this does not establish agreement with ground-truth stage annotations.

evidence_standards.name: Paired-bootstrap uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Report 95% confidence intervals for paired degradation, calculated from 10,000 pair-level bootstrap resamples; the paper describes intervals excluding zero as evidence of degradation and intervals including zero as not excluding zero.

evidence_standards.name: Aggregation and run randomness
evidence_standards.detail: Macro results are equal-weight averages of task-level metrics, not pooled episode estimates. Formal results use fixed base episodes and policy randomness fixed once per episode, shared within each matched pair; the paper does not report multi-seed repetitions or a separate hypothesis test.

datasets.name: LIBERO
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-Object. For the original, unperturbed evaluation, 50 rollouts were run for each of the 10 tasks in each suite. Successful trajectories were identified using LIBERO’s standard binary task-success criterion; behavioural metrics were calculated only for successful trajectories.

datasets.name: LIBERO-Plus
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated using the seven perturbation classes (background, camera, language, lighting, object, robot initial state, and sensor), alongside the unperturbed condition, across the four LIBERO suites. Two rollouts were run per corresponding LIBERO-Plus task variant, except for object perturbation, for which only a single initial state was provided. Each variant was matched to its original LIBERO task; success used LIBERO’s standard binary criterion, and behavioural metrics were calculated only for successful trajectories. Trajectory derivatives used the simulator control frequency of 10 Hz.

baselines.name: π₀.₅
baselines.fair_comparison: Checkpoints were chosen that had been fine-tuned jointly on all LIBERO suites; suite-specific fine-tuned checkpoints were avoided.

baselines.name: VLANeXt
baselines.fair_comparison: Checkpoints were chosen that had been fine-tuned jointly on all LIBERO suites; suite-specific fine-tuned checkpoints were avoided.

baselines.name: OpenVLA-OFT
baselines.fair_comparison: Checkpoints were chosen that had been fine-tuned jointly on all LIBERO suites; suite-specific fine-tuned checkpoints were avoided. Evaluation was limited to the LIBERO-Spatial suite.

metrics.name: Task Success Rate (TSR)
metrics.caveat: Binary TSR can conceal changes in how successful trajectories are executed; the paper reports trajectory-level behavioural metrics alongside it.

metrics.name: Total gripper movement
metrics.caveat: The paper says this can be a proxy for repeated grasp attempts or dropping and re-grasping, but does not precisely diagnose those events; precise diagnosis would require task- and benchmark-specific adaptations.

metrics.name: Median absolute deviation (MAD) of behavioural metrics
metrics.caveat: MAD describes variability, not the change in typical behaviour; the paper reports typical behaviour changes separately using changes in mean trajectory-metric values.

controls.name: Original, unperturbed LIBERO tasks
controls.detail: Successful trajectories on each original LIBERO task are the baseline against which successful trajectories on its matched LIBERO-Plus perturbation variants are compared.
controls.rules_out: A behavioural difference being present in the reference condition itself; a difference against this condition licenses describing a change relative to unperturbed task behaviour.

confounds.name: Reduced variability reflects selective loss of successful recovery trajectories
confounds.detail: Because only successful trajectories are analysed, perturbations could make recovery behaviours fail, leaving disproportionately clean or direct trajectories among the successes and reducing MAD without making the policy’s successful responses intrinsically more consistent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors identify this as a possible explanation and leave distinguishing it for future work.

confounds.name: Reduced variability reflects a narrower policy response to perturbation
confounds.detail: A perturbation could directly cause the policy to generate a narrower range of responses, producing lower MAD even if selective failure of recovery trajectories is not the cause.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors state that distinguishing this explanation from success-selection effects is future work.

confounds.name: Completion-time differences reflect inference latency or GPU contention rather than task execution time
confounds.detail: A wall-clock duration could change because of model inference latency or GPU contention, rather than because the robot takes more or less simulator time to complete the task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Duration is measured as elapsed simulator time between the first and final recorded control steps, using simulator control frequency, rather than wall-clock time.

evidence_standards.name: Two-sided Mann–Whitney U test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction
evidence_standards.detail: Used to assess whether perturbed and baseline trajectory-metric distributions differ, with FDR correction across tasks at α = 0.05.

evidence_standards.name: Spearman rank correlation significance and magnitude interpretation
evidence_standards.detail: For correlations between TSR degradation and behavioural change, the paper reports ρ and p-values and interprets absolute ρ magnitudes as negligible (0.00–0.10), weak (0.10–0.39), moderate (0.40–0.69), strong (0.70–0.89), or very strong (0.90–1.0).

datasets.name: REALM-base
datasets.eval_protocol: 8 pick-place tasks; evaluated under the default setting and 15 perturbations, with 25 rollouts per model/task/perturbation. Task progression scores ordered stages equally from 0 to 1; binary success is also reported.

datasets.name: REALM-articulated
datasets.eval_protocol: 2 articulated cabinet-drawer open/close tasks; evaluated under the default setting and 15 perturbations, with 25 rollouts per model/task/perturbation. Task progression scores ordered stages equally from 0 to 1; binary success is also reported.

datasets.name: REALM real-to-sim validation (DROID platform)
datasets.eval_protocol: Paired real and simulated rollouts on 7 tasks under 5 visual and behavioral perturbations, totaling nearly 800 rollout pairs, using a digital cousin of a previously unseen scene. Compares task progression, Pearson correlation, p-values, and MMRV.

baselines.name: π₀
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same REALM tasks and perturbation conditions as the other evaluated models. Uses an existing open-source checkpoint fine-tuned on DROID.

baselines.name: π₀-FAST
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same REALM tasks and perturbation conditions as the other evaluated models. Uses an existing open-source checkpoint fine-tuned on DROID.

baselines.name: GR00T N1.5
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same REALM tasks and perturbation conditions; the authors fine-tune it to use the same action space as the π models. The paper does not state that training data or training procedures are otherwise matched.

metrics.name: Tiered task progression
metrics.caveat: Binary success gives less granularity; progression scores ordered intermediate stages equally from 0 to 1 and is reported alongside binary success.

metrics.name: Root Mean Squared Deviation (RMSD) in task progression
metrics.caveat: Measures perturbation magnitude while ignoring whether the effect is positive or negative; absolute task progression is reported alongside it.

metrics.name: Binary success rate
metrics.caveat: Does not capture partial progress through a task; tiered task progression is reported alongside it.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation coefficient
metrics.caveat: Correlation does not itself assess consistency of policy rankings; MMRV is also reported.

metrics.name: p-value
metrics.caveat: The paper says lower values are preferred and reports the p-value alongside correlation and MMRV; it reports p<0.001 for real–simulation correlations across settings.

metrics.name: Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV)
metrics.caveat: Assesses policy-ranking consistency rather than the magnitude of task-progression agreement; Pearson correlation is also reported.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity of attention maps
metrics.caveat: Used as an offline indicator of out-of-distribution status, not as a direct task-performance measure.

controls.name: Default task setting
controls.detail: The nominal setting is compared with each perturbed setting; the default is described as close to the DROID training data.
controls.rules_out: A perturbation’s measured task-progression difference being merely the nominal level of performance, by providing an unperturbed reference condition.

confounds.name: Visual gap between simulated renders and real observations
confounds.detail: A visual distribution shift could make the model’s predictions differ in simulation, undermining simulation as a proxy for real-world performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare π₀ attention maps on matched real and simulated video frames; the reported cosine similarity is 0.85.

confounds.name: Misaligned simulated and real robot control
confounds.detail: Even with similar visuals, control mismatch could make simulated action outcomes diverge from real outcomes and invalidate the benchmark as a real-world proxy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Align control using real/sim trajectory replays and system identification; validate task progression on paired real and simulated rollouts, reporting Pearson correlation and MMRV.

confounds.name: Low default performance makes perturbation effects uninformative
confounds.detail: A model that already performs poorly on nominal tasks may show uninformative perturbation effects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors design default settings to be close to DROID training data and focus individual-model generalization discussion on π₀ and π₀-FAST because GR00T has substantially lower progression.

confounds.name: DROID fine-tuning may harm VLM-backbone generalization
confounds.detail: Observed failures could reflect full fine-tuning on DROID harming the VLM backbones’ generalization, rather than only the generalization challenge the benchmark is intended to measure.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors state this as a hypothesis.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed rollout sample size for benchmark task-progression estimates
evidence_standards.detail: Each model/task/perturbation value is averaged over 25 rollouts; the paper describes approximately 4,000 simulation rollouts per model.

evidence_standards.name: Real-to-sim correlation significance
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports a standard two-sided t-test and states p<0.001 for real–simulation correlations in all settings.

evidence_standards.name: Success-rate uncertainty
evidence_standards.detail: Success-rate plots show Bayesian posteriors using a uniform Beta prior and the observed data.

evidence_standards.name: Perturbation-effect variability
evidence_standards.detail: RMSD figure error bars show deviation in effects across models and tasks; tighter bars indicate more consistent effects. The paper does not specify a seed count or a numerical margin for treating results as ties.

datasets.name: SimplerEnv
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated the first 500 VLATest-generated scenes for each of four tasks, using the Google robot for Pick Up and Move Near and WidowX for Put In and Put On. A fixed environment seed kept initial scenes consistent across models; scenes had randomly selected target objects, 0–3 confounding objects, and at least 0.15 m between objects, with default lighting and camera pose. Success required: Pick Up, grasp and lift the correct object at least 0.02 m for five consecutive frames; Move Near, place A within 0.05 m of B; Put On, leave A balanced on B; Put In, place A fully inside B. Successful executions were also labeled high, medium, or low quality by experts.

datasets.name: VLATest
datasets.eval_protocol: Replicated its evaluation using the first 500 generated scenes per task in SimplerEnv, across the same four tasks and two robot embodiments. The symbolic success oracle was used, and successful executions were additionally assessed for quality by human experts; the authors identified false positives from the oracle, such as objects already positioned at the destination.

baselines.name: OpenVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same fixed-seed scenes, tasks, and robot embodiments as the other evaluated models; the study used the authors’ HuggingFace base checkpoint.

baselines.name: π0
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same fixed-seed scenes, tasks, and robot embodiments as the other evaluated models; the authors’ Fractal and Bridge checkpoints were used for the corresponding tasks.

baselines.name: SpatialVLA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same fixed-seed scenes, tasks, and robot embodiments as the other evaluated models; the study used the authors’ checkpoint pretrained on a mixture of the two datasets.

metrics.name: Task success rate
metrics.caveat: Binary success does not capture execution quality; successful tasks could be labeled low quality by experts. The paper reports expert quality labels alongside success.

metrics.name: Human-labeled task quality (high, medium, low)
metrics.caveat: Expert judgments may be subjective; the paper reports Cohen’s kappa agreement and used a third expert to resolve disagreements.

metrics.name: A-PI (Action Position Instability)
metrics.caveat: Large action changes can reflect purposeful high-speed movement rather than instability; the paper also evaluates second-order A-VI to distinguish changes in motion dynamics.

metrics.name: EV (Execution Variability)
metrics.caveat: For near-deterministic policies, repeated inferences can be identical and EV becomes uninformative; it also has the highest inference overhead because it requires multiple model executions. The paper reports correlation and overhead results alongside it.

metrics.name: TCP-PI (Trajectory Position Instability)
metrics.caveat: Large positional changes can reflect high-speed rather than erratic motion; the paper also evaluates second-order TCP-VI.

metrics.name: OT (Optimal Trajectory Difference)
metrics.caveat: Its assumption that effective execution continually reduces distance to the goal can fail with detours, obstacle avoidance, or dynamic adjustments; the paper notes that it is mainly suitable for simulation/offline evaluation. It reports this alongside its discrimination results.

metrics.name: Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ)
metrics.caveat: Correlation was computed after aggregating step-level metric values to a trajectory mean; results depend on task and model. The paper reports p-values and interprets correlation magnitudes using stated thresholds.

metrics.name: Mann–Whitney U test
metrics.caveat: Used for non-normally distributed values; the paper reports Vargha–Delaney Â12 effect sizes alongside significance.

metrics.name: Inference time and execution overhead
metrics.caveat: Timing may be affected by hardware; experiments for each model were run on one server, and the paper reports mean and standard deviation.

confounds.name: Object orientation, rather than the measured metric behavior, may explain low quality in Move Near
confounds.detail: Some executions were labeled low quality because the object’s final orientation was incorrect, although the proposed metrics may not capture that aspect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors recomputed correlations after removing low-quality Move Near cases attributed to incorrect object orientation. The analysis showed the metrics did not adequately capture this factor; it was not ruled out.

confounds.name: Server hardware differences may explain timing differences
confounds.detail: π0 ran on a different server from OpenVLA and SpatialVLA, so raw execution-time comparisons could reflect hardware rather than model or metric costs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: All experiments for a given model ran exclusively on the same server, and the authors conducted analyses per model rather than relying on direct cross-model comparisons of raw metric values.

confounds.name: Human quality labels may reflect annotator subjectivity
confounds.detail: The reported relationships with quality could depend on inconsistent expert judgments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Two domain experts labeled the cases; agreement was assessed with Cohen’s kappa (reported as 85%), and a third domain expert resolved disagreements.

confounds.name: Model differences may reflect training-data heterogeneity
confounds.detail: Differences in fine-tuning data across tasks could account for measured model behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors state that they mitigated this by using models fine-tuned with the same dataset across different tasks.

confounds.name: Robot embodiment may explain performance differences across tasks
confounds.detail: The Google robot was used for Pick Up and Move Near, while WidowX was used for Put On and Put In, so cross-task differences may reflect embodiment as well as task or model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares models within the same tasks and embodiments, but does not isolate embodiment effects; it explicitly notes embodiment may influence overall performance.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed environment seed
evidence_standards.detail: The same seed initialized environments across models to keep initial scene states consistent; the paper does not report multiple random seeds or repeated evaluation runs.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation procedure
evidence_standards.detail: Two domain experts labeled successful executions as high, medium, or low quality; disagreements were resolved by a third expert. Agreement was assessed with Cohen’s kappa and reported as 85%. Labeling was spread across 15 days, with at most 160 cases per session.

evidence_standards.name: RQ2 correlation decision rule
evidence_standards.detail: Spearman rank correlation was used on trajectory-level mean metric values; p < 0.05 indicated statistical significance. Correlation was interpreted as none for ρ < 0.10, weak for 0.10–0.29, moderate for 0.29–0.49, and strong for ρ > 0.49.

evidence_standards.name: RQ3 difference decision rule
evidence_standards.detail: Shapiro–Wilk was used to assess distributions; because values were non-normal, the authors used Mann–Whitney U, treating p < 0.05 as statistically significant, and reported Vargha–Delaney Â12 effect sizes.

evidence_standards.name: Inference-time reporting
evidence_standards.detail: Inference time and metric overhead are reported as mean and standard deviation.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated inference setting for EV
evidence_standards.detail: EV used four inference samples, the maximum the authors could load on their hardware; the paper does not specify a decoding setting for the reported results.

datasets.name: Table30
datasets.eval_protocol: 30 real-robot table tasks across the listed machine types. For each rollout, a tester matches the scene to an initial frame from a reference episode; reference episodes are held out from training. Each task receives 10 rollouts. Reported metrics are task success rate and progress score. Each task has stages worth a total of 10 points; completed stages earn their points, retries deduct 0.5 points, and a rollout terminates if a stage score becomes negative or failed successive retries exceed 4. A task is counted successful if all critical stages are completed; non-critical stages may be skipped.

baselines.name: π0.5 (task-specific)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same Table30 tasks and benchmark protocol. For this setting, each model is trained separately per task using all provided demonstration data; the paper does not specify matched training compute across methods.

baselines.name: π0 (task-specific)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same Table30 tasks and benchmark protocol. For this setting, each model is trained separately per task using all provided demonstration data; the paper does not specify matched training compute across methods.

baselines.name: CogACT (task-specific)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same Table30 tasks and benchmark protocol. For this setting, each model is trained separately per task using all provided demonstration data; the paper does not specify matched training compute across methods.

baselines.name: π0.5/multi (generalist)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same Table30 tasks and benchmark protocol. The generalist setting trains on about 50 samples per task mixed only across tasks using the same type of machine.

baselines.name: π0/multi (generalist)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same Table30 tasks and benchmark protocol. The generalist setting trains on about 50 samples per task mixed only across tasks using the same type of machine.

metrics.name: Success rate (SR)
metrics.caveat: The paper says SR alone is insufficient: a hard task can show substantial progress but fail at the last step, while SR does not reflect retries or imperfections on easier tasks. It reports progress score alongside SR.

metrics.name: Progress score
metrics.caveat: A task can succeed but receive a low score after many retries, or fail at the last step while retaining a high score. The paper reports SR alongside it. Scores use stage points, with 0.5 deducted per retry.

confounds.name: Tester-dependent scene preparation can change measured performance
confounds.detail: Different object choices and placements can produce large run-to-run differences; adaptive testers may exploit favorable object positions (the “sweet spot” effect), while inexperienced testers may set up scenes inconsistently.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares experienced, ignorant, and adaptive testers, then uses visual task reproduction: testers match each rollout’s initial scene to a reference episode image held out from training. It reports this setup as more stable than experienced testers.

confounds.name: Background or environmental changes could explain differences in outcomes
confounds.detail: Lighting changes and camera-extrinsic drift remain uncontrolled and could affect the evaluation results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A proof-of-concept comparison runs models on original and manually augmented or corrupted images; the authors report that model outputs largely remain consistent. They do not report a task-success comparison for this check.

confounds.name: Submissions may not run the model they claim to run
confounds.detail: Because inference runs on the user’s side, a user could use a different solution, individually tuned models instead of a claimed generalist, or human-in-the-loop assistance, making the reported result unrelated to the claimed model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No verification measurement is reported; the authors state they cannot check the model being run and rely on user integrity and voluntary release of models and code.

confounds.name: Models may overfit to the fixed reference test cases
confounds.detail: The fixed test distribution used for visual scene reproduction could let submissions overfit to those particular reference cases.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No specific measurement is described; the authors state that they have not observed this overfitting in practice.

evidence_standards.name: 10 rollouts per task
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports SR and progress score from 10 task rollouts. It does not specify seeds, uncertainty intervals, a statistical test, or a threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: PhysicalAI WorldModel-Synthetic Autonomous Driving Scenarios
datasets.eval_protocol: 50 curated lane-change scenarios; no train/test split is specified. Uses the front-wide camera with four context frames at 0.5 s stride, resized to 576×320. Scenarios are selected for a detected lead vehicle within a ±4 m lateral band and 5–40 m range (preferring approximately 20 m), and deduplicated against environment-permutation expansions; cases without a qualifying detection are rejected. Evaluates open-loop 64-waypoint trajectories at 10 Hz using paired baseline and steered runs with identical seeds.

metrics.name: Average Displacement Error (ADE)
metrics.caveat: Can understate operationally important late-horizon shifts; the paper reports maximum lateral shift alongside it. Neither ADE nor larger displacement is a driving-quality score.

metrics.name: Maximum lateral shift over the horizon
metrics.caveat: Reported as a more faithful summary than ADE for late-horizon shifts in this setting; it is not a driving-quality score.

metrics.name: Chain-of-Causation (CoC) change rate under exact string match
metrics.caveat: Unchanged CoC text does not demonstrate robustness to the intervention: the exposure audit found zero biased CoC prefill or decode calls.

metrics.name: Cliff’s δ
metrics.caveat: Measures detectability rather than effect magnitude; δ=1.0 is largely forced by the paired zero-bias gate making the control ADE exactly zero. The paper reports ADE dose-response values alongside it.

metrics.name: Shift direction relative to the attended actor’s side
metrics.caveat: Computed only while the actor remains ahead under a constant-velocity actor model; the paper treats the directional result as qualitative and reports the actor-ahead fraction and a per-clip validity threshold.

controls.name: Paired zero-bias condition
controls.detail: The same model is run with head_scale=0 using the identical seed and deterministic-algorithms configuration as the steered run; the zero-bias gate requires exact baseline trajectory reproduction (ADE=0).
controls.rules_out: A trajectory difference caused by the bias being absent, or by between-run sampler randomness under the paired seed; it does not establish actor specificity.

controls.name: Layer-subset ablations
controls.detail: At head_scale=4, compares first_8, mid_8, last_4, last_8, last_16, and all_layers hook placements.
controls.rules_out: That the observed response is independent of which or how many layers are hooked; these comparisons assess layer localization and depth accumulation, not actor specificity.

confounds.name: Trajectory changes could be diffusion-sampler stochasticity rather than an effect of the bias
confounds.detail: The cross-seed baseline variation is much larger than the reported steering effect, so an unpaired difference could arise from sampling noise.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Paired baseline and steered runs use identical seeds and deterministic-algorithms settings; same-seed repeats are bit-identical and the zero-bias gate gives ADE=0. In a separate check, 3 cases at 5 seeds each had a mean paired effect of 0.107 m versus 3.23 m mean cross-seed baseline distance.

confounds.name: CoC invariance could be interpreted as robustness of the reasoning pathway to attention steering
confounds.detail: That interpretation would look the same if the reasoning pathway were never perturbed.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The per-call exposure audit found zero biased CoC prefill and decode calls; the mask-based intervention applied only during diffusion action-decoder passes. The paper therefore attributes CoC invariance to non-exposure, not demonstrated robustness.

confounds.name: The trajectory response could be sensitivity to token count or image position rather than to the identity of the attended actor
confounds.detail: A response to the intervention alone would look like actor-specific steering even if the same number of biased tokens elsewhere, or tokens depicting something else, produced it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The authors explicitly acknowledge that they ran no matched-control interventions; they identify shifted or mirrored boxes, background regions, a second vehicle, and scattered token sets as needed controls, and claim no actor specificity.

confounds.name: Detector or actor-grounding variation could account for trajectory differences
confounds.detail: The paper notes that detector variance can be indistinguishable from bias variance in trajectory deltas, and that parked, out-of-frame, truncated, or occluded vehicles can make actor grounding misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The study uses curated authored lane-change scenarios with an unambiguous lead actor held in frame, reuses the same scenario in paired runs, and verifies mapped token indices against tokenizer video-token spans. The paper limits external validity and does not claim this resolves the issue for recorded logs.

evidence_standards.name: Paired-seed reproducibility and zero-bias gate
evidence_standards.detail: Baseline and steered runs share an identical seed and deterministic-algorithms configuration; the zero-bias condition must reproduce the baseline trajectory exactly (ADE=0). A noise-floor check uses 3 cases at 5 seeds each. The paper reports no confidence intervals or practical equivalence margin.

evidence_standards.name: Paired statistical testing for dose-response comparisons
evidence_standards.detail: Uses Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction; reports all nonzero bias conditions as significant against paired zero bias (p≪10⁻¹⁰) and reports Cliff’s δ. The paper cautions that δ=1.0 is largely a consequence of the zero-bias gate, so it is not treated as evidence of effect magnitude.

evidence_standards.name: CoC decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: The default CoC temperature is T=0.01; CoC invariance is also checked at T∈{0.3, 0.7, 1.0} on a five-case subset. The paper notes that this does not establish robustness because the CoC path was not exposed to the intervention.

datasets.name: AeroManip-VLA (PrepareGroceries)
datasets.eval_protocol: Simulation evaluation of Pick and Place for 8 objects (16 skill–object combinations); reports success rate and binomial standard error, with Mean S.R. the unweighted average over the 16 combinations. The number of evaluation episodes is not stated.

datasets.name: AeroManip-VLA (TidyHouse)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for trajectory-diversity and execution-efficiency analyses. Diversity coverage and velocity-direction entropy are estimated from 200 random subsets of 80 episodes per policy; execution-time statistics are conditioned on successful episodes.

baselines.name: ACT
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the other baselines on the paper's aerial manipulation dataset; no further matched training conditions are stated.

baselines.name: Diffusion Policy (DP)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the other baselines on the paper's aerial manipulation dataset; no further matched training conditions are stated.

baselines.name: π₀
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the other baselines on the paper's aerial manipulation dataset; no further matched training conditions are stated.

baselines.name: π₀.₅
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with the other baselines on the paper's aerial manipulation dataset; no further matched training conditions are stated.

metrics.name: Success rate
metrics.caveat: A single aggregate can obscure differences across skills and objects; the paper also reports skill- and object-level rates.

metrics.name: Mean S.R.
metrics.caveat: It is an unweighted average over 16 Pick/Place–object combinations; the paper also reports the individual combination rates.

metrics.name: Deviation from each policy’s own mean path
Spatial coverage
metrics.caveat: Measured by occupied 0.05 × 0.05 cells; estimated from 200 random subsets of 80 episodes per policy, with mean and 95% interval reported.

metrics.name: Velocity-direction entropy
metrics.caveat: Computed over 36 bins; estimated from 200 random subsets of 80 episodes per policy, with mean and 95% interval reported.

metrics.name: Time to success
metrics.caveat: Statistics are conditioned on successful episodes, so they measure execution efficiency rather than end-to-end demonstration collection throughput; the paper also reports phase times and episode-length distributions.

metrics.name: Learning efficiency
metrics.caveat: Training interaction requirements are distinct from execution efficiency; the paper reports demonstration transitions for BC and environment interactions for PPO.

confounds.name: Greater trajectory diversity could come simply from taking longer or more circuitous routes
confounds.detail: That would make PPO’s more diverse successful trajectories an apparent benefit of route duration rather than a better execution strategy.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures execution time and phase times for successful episodes; PPO is substantially faster than the expert and BC, especially in the approach phase.

evidence_standards.name: One training seed per method
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states this for the Figure 2 learning-efficiency comparison; it does not report multi-seed variance or a statistical test there.

evidence_standards.name: Binomial standard error for success rates
evidence_standards.detail: Table 1 reports success rates with binomial standard errors; no statistical test or threshold for deciding a difference is real is stated.

evidence_standards.name: Mean and 95% interval for trajectory-diversity estimates
evidence_standards.detail: Coverage and velocity-direction entropy use 200 random subsets of 80 episodes per policy; no statistical test or decision threshold is stated.
